analysis.one_liner: Requires the SEC to prove each new rule's benefits outweigh its costs before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write a cost-benefit mandate into securities law. Before the SEC could issue any new rule, it would have to identify the problem the rule addresses, prove with the agency's Chief Economist that benefits justify costs, consider alternatives including doing nothing, and periodically re-review and potentially repeal existing rules. Rules written by self-regulatory bodies like the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board could not take effect unless the SEC first certified they met the same test.
analysis.who_benefits: The securities firms, exchanges, asset managers, and public companies that are the main subjects of SEC rulemaking would benefit, because every new rule would face a formal burden-of-proof hurdle and existing rules could be reconsidered and repealed. Over the long run, investors might benefit somewhat from clearer, better-justified rules, but the primary beneficiaries are regulated firms facing lighter oversight.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Securities firms and regulated financial companies

how_it_helps.text: The SEC could adopt a rule only after a 'reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify the costs,' a legal standard that regulated firms can challenge in court to slow or undo rules they oppose.

The bill requires the SEC to consider alternatives to any regulation, including not regulating at all, and to weigh impacts on market liquidity, small businesses, investor choice, and U.S. economic competitiveness — considerations that tilt against interventionist rules such as market-structure or disclosure mandates.

The SEC would have to periodically review existing rules as potentially 'outmoded, ineffective, insufficient, or excessively burdensome' and modify, streamline, or repeal them accordingly, opening the door to rolling back existing investor protections.

Rules adopted by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board, FINRA, and similar self-regulators could not take effect unless the SEC first certified they met the same cost-benefit requirements, adding a layer of review that would slow industry-policing rules.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary investors and retirement savers, who rely on SEC rules for honest disclosures, fair market practices, and protection against fraud, would bear the cost in the form of slower, weaker, and more easily challenged investor-protection rules. The SEC itself would lose discretion, spending its resources producing cost-benefit analyses and post-rule reviews instead of enforcement and rulemaking.

drawbacks.text: The cost-benefit requirement gives regulated firms a litigation weapon: a court challenge on whether the SEC's benefit analysis was 'reasoned' can delay or invalidate a rule for years, which is a major reason financial-industry groups have historically backed similar regulatory-accountability bills.

Many benefits of investor protection — fraud deterred, honest markets maintained — are hard to quantify, so rules whose benefits are diffuse could be re-drawn or repealed even when they keep retirement savings safe.

On the other side, an honest supporter would acknowledge that the SEC has sometimes issued sweeping rules with thin economic analysis, and a formal review-and-repeal cycle could catch genuinely outdated or duplicative rules that burden small firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A few of the bill's elements — plain-language rules, considering whether a regulation is duplicative, periodic review of outdated rules — sound reasonable on their face. But the core mechanism shifts the burden of proof so that the default is inaction, and it hands regulated firms a legal pathway to challenge any rule they dislike. Given that the SEC's rules are the main guardrails over the markets where most Americans keep their retirement savings, the likely cost to investor protection outweighs the administrative tidiness the bill promises.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the final weeks of the 117th Congress and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ann Wagner introduced the bill on December 15, 2022, in the final weeks of the 117th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced, and no further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was recorded.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, from either party.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and bills that do not advance die at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary investors came out ahead, because the SEC kept its existing authority to write and enforce investor-protection rules without the added burden-of-proof mandate. The securities industry is in the same position as before: it avoided neither the bill's lighter-touch regime nor anything new, since nothing changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary investors, since SEC authority stayed intact

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 117th Congress by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up; it was referred on December 15, 2022, and received no hearing, markup, or committee vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so support or opposition beyond the single Republican sponsor was never tested.

industries.industry: Securities firms, exchanges, and asset managers
industries.note: If passed, the bill would have made every SEC rule face a formal benefits-justify-costs test and an 'including not regulating' alternatives analysis, and would let existing rules be re-reviewed and repealed. These firms' interest runs against the public's in this bill: the rules they would face are the ones that police fair dealing with retail investors and retirement savers.

industries.industry: Self-regulatory organizations (FINRA, Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board, PCAOB)
industries.note: The bill would add an SEC certification step before their rules take effect, slowing their industry-policing work, while a 'sense of Congress' would have the accounting oversight board follow the same cost-benefit discipline. The public effect is likewise two-sided: delay in policing rules, but a check on self-regulators' power.

industries.industry: Public companies subject to SEC disclosure rules
industries.note: Disclosure and market-structure rules would face a higher burden of proof and potential repeal under the periodic review mandate. Their interest in lighter disclosure runs against investors who rely on that disclosure.
